meta.title: Who really said "What's the quickest way to become a millionaire? Borrow fivers off everyone you meet"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Richard Branson everywhere, but no book, speech or interview has ever been produced. The trail ends at an unsourced 2007 Wikiquote edit.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What's the quickest way to become a millionaire? Borrow fivers off everyone you meet'?
meta.ogDescription: No source has ever been found for this Branson quip. The earliest trace is a Wikiquote edit of 19 January 2007, already filed under 'Unsourced'.

answer.label: Unsourced — never traced to Branson
answer.authorDates: Circulating under Richard Branson’s name since January 2007 · no primary source ever produced
answer.sourceLine: Every trail leads back to quote-aggregator sites and, behind them, a single uncited Wikiquote edit made on 19 January 2007 — which filed the line under a heading that already read Unsourced. No book, broadcast, speech, interview or article containing this sentence has ever been identified, and Wikiquote moved it off Branson’s page in December 2008 for exactly that reason. That is not proof he never said it; it is proof that nobody has been able to show he did.

source.excerpt: What’s the quickest way to become a millionaire? Borrow fivers off everyone you meet.
trail: 19 January 2007 — the earliest trace we can find anywhere. An editor adds the line to Wikiquote’s Richard Branson page with no edit summary and no citation, directly under a section heading that already reads “Unsourced.” That revision is still on the public record ↗.

6 December 2008 — Wikiquote cleans house. An editor moves the unsourced quotes off the article and creates Talk:Richard Branson ↗ with the summary “Transferred unsourced quotes to talk page.” The fivers line goes with them and has never come back.

Ever since — the quote spreads through commercial aggregators instead. AZQuotes runs it under Branson’s name ↗ with no book, date, interview or source of any kind, and dozens of listicles copy from that layer.

Nearly two decades on, the line is still absent from Wikiquote’s sourced Branson page ↗, from his published books as far as anyone has shown, and from every documented interview we could reach. The credit has travelled a long way on nothing.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to show. No book, transcript, broadcast or article containing this sentence has ever been identified, so the line exists only as a free-floating epigram passed between quote sites.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted here, because no source work has ever been identified. If Branson did say this in a modern interview or broadcast, that article or recording would be in copyright to its publisher; because nothing has been produced, quotle.info makes no public-domain claim for this wording.

externalLinks.label: Talk:Richard Branson (Wikiquote)
externalLinks.what: The holding pen where this quote actually lives. Wikiquote states it no longer allows unsourced quotations and invites anyone with a reliable, precise source to move the line back to the article. Nobody has.

externalLinks.label: Wikiquote revision of 19 January 2007
externalLinks.what: The earliest appearance we can locate anywhere. The line is added with no edit summary and no citation, directly beneath a section heading reading “Unsourced.”

author.name: Richard Branson
author.heading: About Richard Branson
author.metaLine: Born 18 July 1950 · English entrepreneur, founder of the Virgin Group
author.bio: Richard Branson launched the magazine Student in 1966, built a mail-order record operation into the Virgin Records shops of the early 1970s, and started Virgin Atlantic in 1984 — the spine of what became the sprawling Virgin Group. He is also a gifted self-promoter with a taste for the deflating one-liner, which is precisely why sourceless gags about money stick to his name so readily. His autobiography Losing My Virginity (1998) remains the closest thing to a primary record of how he actually talks about getting rich.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is not the usual case of the wrong person being credited. It is the case where nobody — not Wikiquote’s editors, not the commercial quote sites that run it daily — can show that anyone said it.

items.why: Aggregators run the line under his name with nothing attached: AZQuotes carries it bare ↗, no book, no date, no interview. Wikiquote reached the same dead end far earlier and parked it in its unsourced holding pen ↗, where it has stayed.

Branson’s genuinely famous millionaire quip is a different sentence — “If you want to be a Millionaire, start with a billion dollars and launch a new airline” — and the two get blurred together in listicles. Wikiquote flags even that one for a better source ↗, but it does carry a secondary citation — a P. Greenberg MSNBC piece quoted in a 2001 Harvard Business School reprint. The fivers line has never had a citation of any kind.

items.scope: The ancestry of that other line, not of this one
items.why: The ‘start with a large fortune’ structure behind the airline quip is not Branson’s invention: Quote Investigator tentatively credits the singer Leo Fuld with a February 1950 instance ↗ and does not mention Branson anywhere. No comparable research exists for the ‘borrow fivers’ line, which QI has not investigated.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position is that this is an unsourced quotation rather than a debunked one. It has been credited to Richard Branson since at least 19 January 2007 ↗, and in all the time since, no book, broadcast or article has been produced to support it.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: Branson belongs to the small set of names — alongside Einstein, Churchill, Twain and Jobs — that act as magnets for orphan quotations. A line only has to sound like the person for the internet to file it under them permanently, and a self-deprecating gag about getting rich sounds exactly like the Branson of the public imagination: the billionaire who plays the chancer.

The joke itself is the sort of bar-room arithmetic gag whose punchline is that the maths technically works — borrow a fiver from two hundred thousand people and you are, on paper, a millionaire. What makes it worth flagging is not that it is funny but that nearly two decades of repetition have never produced a date, a stage, a broadcast or a page number.
context.detailsSummary: Why ‘unsourced’ is not the same as ‘fake’
detailsBody: A debunked quotation is one where somebody has found the real author, or shown the supposed speaker was demonstrably elsewhere. This is a different category: a line for which no evidence exists in either direction. Branson has given thousands of interviews across sixty years of public life, many of them on regional radio and television that was never transcribed, so absence of a record is genuinely weaker evidence here than it would be for a writer whose complete works are indexed.

What can be said flatly is that the burden has never been met. Wikiquote’s editors looked, could not source it, and moved it out of the article — the standard route by which unverifiable lines are quarantined rather than deleted. Every commercial quote site that carries it does so without a citation of any kind. Until someone produces the interview, this page treats the credit as unsupported.
context.pull: Nobody has ever produced a source — only a chain of sites quoting one another.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote holds "What's the quickest way to become a millionaire? Borrow fivers off everyone you meet." on Talk:Richard Branson, under a notice stating Wikiquote no longer allows unsourced quotations and inviting anyone with a reliable, precise source to move it back to the article.
The 19 January 2007 revision of Wikiquote's Richard Branson page contains the quote, placed under the section heading "Unsourced" with no citation.

The revision history of Talk:Richard Branson shows the page was created on 6 December 2008 by user InvisibleSun with the edit summary "Transferred unsourced quotes to talk page.", with a further move of unsourced quotes by Ningauble on 22 July 2010.

Wikiquote's main Richard Branson article does not contain the 'borrow fivers' quote; it does carry "If you want to be a Millionaire, start with a billion dollars and launch a new airline", sourced to 'P. Greenberg, "Why JetBlue will be different," MSNBC as cited in Gittell and O'Reilly (October, 2001) Harvard Business School Press Reprint No. 9-801-354' and carrying a {{source}} flag that renders as [citation needed].
AZQuotes displays the quote credited to Richard Branson with no source, book, date or interview given.

Quote Investigator traces the 'make a small fortune / start with a large fortune' joke family to a 9 February 1950 Courier-Post column by Earl Wilson and tentatively credits singer Leo Fuld with initiating it; the article does not mention Richard Branson.
Richard Branson was born 18 July 1950, is English, launched Student magazine in 1966, opened Virgin Records stores in 1972, and founded Virgin Atlantic in 1984.
The Internet Archive hosts a borrowable copy of Richard Branson's Losing My Virginity, Times Business, 1998.
